title: Mordecai the Jew, Second to the King
summary: The book closes with a brief epilogue. King Xerxes imposes tribute across his empire to its farthest shores, and the narrator points to the Persian royal chronicles for the full record of his power and of Mordecai's greatness. Mordecai, second only to the king, is honored by his people and remembered for seeking their good and speaking peace to all his kin.
story: Chapter 9 ended with the establishment of Purim and Esther's decree confirming it. These three verses round off the story by returning to where it began: with the king, his power, and his empire. But the focus has shifted. In chapter 1 the reader met Xerxes displaying his wealth for 180 days; here the book's last words belong to Mordecai the Jew, who once sat in sackcloth outside the gate and now stands next to the throne. The story that began with the Jews' destruction decreed ends with a Jew in the highest office under the king, using that office for the welfare of his people. The Old Testament's historical narrative of the Persian period continues in Ezra and Nehemiah, which tell of the Jews who returned to Jerusalem.
historical:
Xerxes ruled from 486 to 465 BC. His great invasion of Greece, launched in 480 BC, ended in defeat at the naval battle of Salamis that year and the land battle of Plataea in 479 BC. The book says nothing of these wars, but the notice that he imposed tribute throughout the land, even to its farthest shores (literally, the coastlands or islands of the sea), fits the picture of a king consolidating revenue and control across a vast empire. Tribute from subject peoples was the financial backbone of the Persian state, and the reliefs at Persepolis show delegations from many nations bringing gifts to the king.

The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia has not survived, and nothing like it has been recovered. Historians have searched Persian-period records for Mordecai. A cuneiform tablet from about the time of Xerxes mentions an official named Marduka serving at Susa, and the name appears in other Persian administrative texts, but whether any of these refers to the Mordecai of this book cannot be shown. The book's historical character is debated: some scholars regard it as history, others as a historical story built around real Persian customs, and many take positions between.
cultural:
The phrase are they not written in the book of the chronicles echoes the formula used again and again in the books of Kings for the rulers of Israel and Judah. For a Jewish reader, the effect is to place Mordecai's deeds alongside the records of kings, and to present his service in a foreign court as part of the history of God's people. Being second to the king was a known office in ancient empires; Joseph held such a position under Pharaoh, and Daniel was raised high under Babylonian and Persian rulers. Mordecai joins that line of Jews who served foreign kings faithfully without abandoning their identity.

The final description of Mordecai uses the language of a good ruler in Israel's tradition. Seeking the good of his people and speaking peace describe not personal ambition but responsible leadership, the kind of service the prophets and wisdom writers held up as the purpose of power.
literary: The epilogue is short and formal, like the closing notices of reigns in the books of Kings. It frames the whole book: chapter 1 opened with Xerxes' power and splendor, and chapter 10 returns to his power, but ends with Mordecai. The word greatness, used of the king's splendor in chapter 1 (1:4), is now used of the honor given to Mordecai. The last verse gathers titles and qualities in a single sentence: second to the king, great among the Jews, favored by his many kinsmen, seeking good, speaking peace. Its final word in Hebrew points to his descendants or kin, leaving the reader with the continuing life of a people who were meant to be destroyed.

outline.t: Xerxes imposes tribute across the empire
The record of the king's power and Mordecai's greatness
Mordecai, second to the king, seeks his people's good

doctrines.note: The book ends with the threatened people secure and one of their own raised to power. The hidden hand at work through the whole story has brought the Jews from a decree of death to a place of peace under a foreign king.
Xerxes' empire and his tribute frame the ending, but the last word goes to a servant who uses power for others. The contrast hints at the Bible's larger picture of true rule as service.

words.note: Mishneh, second. Mordecai was second to the king, the highest position a subject could hold. The word is used of a second in rank or a copy, and here it marks the complete reversal of his earlier position outside the gate.

Shalom, peace, wholeness, well-being. Mordecai spoke peace to all his people. The word means far more than the absence of war: it describes flourishing, security, and right relationships, the welfare that a good ruler seeks for those under him.

Darash, to seek or inquire. Mordecai sought the good of his people. The verb is often used of seeking God or seeking someone's welfare, and here it describes the purpose of Mordecai's power: not his own advancement but his people's good.

Mas, forced labor or tribute. Xerxes imposed tribute on the land and the coastlands. The word elsewhere describes the forced labor Solomon imposed and Israel suffered under Egypt, and here it reminds the reader that the Jews still live under an empire's demands.

christ: Mordecai, raised from humiliation to be second to the king and using his authority to seek his people's good and speak peace, is a figure whose pattern the New Testament sees fulfilled far more fully in Jesus. The connection is thematic: the book does not present Mordecai as a messianic figure. But the humbled one who is exalted and rules for the welfare of others is the shape of Christ's own story, and Paul writes that Jesus “came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). Where Mordecai spoke peace to his kinsmen under a foreign king, Christ makes peace between God and humanity and between peoples once divided, and he rules not as second to any earthly throne but at the right hand of God.
questions: Mordecai is remembered not for his power but for seeking his people's good. How would you want your own influence to be remembered?
The Jews in Esther live faithfully under a foreign empire without political control. What can Christians learn from them about living as a minority?
Looking back over the whole book of Esther, where do you see God at work though he is never named?
